title: Same $30, two percentages
hook: A shop adds 50% to a $60 jacket. What share of the price is profit?

knows: what a percentage of a number is
doesNotKnow: that markup is measured against cost and margin against the selling price

objective: The learner can say that a $30 profit on a $60 cost is a 50% markup but a 33% margin of the $90 price, and that margin stays below 100% however large the markup.

claims.text: A $60 jacket with a 50% markup sells for $90, with $30 profit; $30 is 50% of the cost and about 33.3% of the price.
Markup is profit divided by cost; margin is profit divided by the selling price.
claims.source: Standard retail definitions (retail accounting): markup = (price - cost) / cost; gross margin = (price - cost) / price.

claims.text: Margin equals markup divided by (1 + markup), so it stays below 100% however large the markup.
claims.source: profit/price = (m x cost) / (cost x (1 + m)) = m / (1 + m) < 1 for every m (algebra).

claims.text: At a 100% markup the $60 jacket sells for $120 and the $60 profit is half the price.
The lesson is a model: one jacket, a fixed $60 cost, no other costs, illustrative numbers.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Model: one jacket, $60 cost, no other costs'.

recall.question: A shop buys a lamp for $40 and adds a 100% markup. What share of the selling price is profit?
recall.why: Price is 40 x 2 = $80, profit $40, and 40 / 80 = 50% of the price. A 100% markup is a 50% margin.
